meta.titre: Electrode Potentials: standard hydrogen electrode, cell emf and feasibility

sections.contenu_markdown: A battery seller in Douala explains that a car battery and a torch battery both work because chemical half-reactions push electrons around a circuit with different strengths. A 12 V car battery costs about 25 000 FCFA, and the voltage it can deliver depends on which half-reactions are used inside it. Standard electrode potentials give chemists a table that predicts the voltage of a cell, which species are good oxidising or reducing agents, and whether a given redox reaction is feasible. At GCE Advanced Level you are expected to calculate cell emf values, to choose the positive electrode correctly and to say what a positive emf does and does not tell you.

items: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons; an oxidising agent is reduced, a reducing agent is oxidised.
A redox equation is balanced so that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained, and so that atoms and charges balance.
In a metal-ion half-cell the equilibrium $\mathrm{M^{n+}(aq) + ne^- \rightleftharpoons M(s)}$ is set up at the surface of the metal.

sections.titre: Standard electrode potentials, cell emf and feasibility of reactions
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Standard electrode potential, $E^{\ominus}$.** The standard electrode potential of a half-cell is the emf of a cell in which the half-cell, under standard conditions, is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode, the hydrogen electrode being the reference on the left. It is always quoted for the **reduction** half-equation, $\mathrm{M^{n+}(aq) + ne^- \rightleftharpoons M(s)}$.

**Standard conditions:** temperature 298 K; every ion in solution at concentration $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$; every gas at a pressure of 1 atm (101 kPa); metals and solids pure.

**The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)** is a piece of platinum coated with platinum black dipping in $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ hydrogen ions, with hydrogen gas at 1 atm bubbling over the platinum: $\mathrm{2H^+(aq) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons H_2(g)}$. Its potential is **defined** as $0.00\ \mathrm{V}$; all other values are measured against it.

**Reading the table.** The more positive $E^{\ominus}$ is, the stronger the oxidising agent on the left-hand side of the half-equation. The more negative $E^{\ominus}$ is, the stronger the reducing agent on the right-hand side.

**Calculating the emf of a cell.** The half-cell with the more positive $E^{\ominus}$ is the positive electrode, where reduction occurs; the other half-cell is the negative electrode, where oxidation occurs. Electrons flow in the external wire from the negative to the positive electrode.

$$E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}(\text{positive electrode}) - E^{\ominus}(\text{negative electrode})$$

The salt bridge (filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate solution, for example) completes the circuit by allowing ions, not electrons, to move.

**Combining half-equations.** Write both half-equations as reductions, reverse the one with the more negative $E^{\ominus}$, multiply the equations so that the electrons cancel, then add. **$E^{\ominus}$ values are not multiplied** by these factors, because a potential is energy per unit charge and does not depend on the amount of substance.

**Feasibility.** A reaction is predicted to be feasible under standard conditions if $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} > 0$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When both species of the half-cell are in solution or one is a gas, as in $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$ or $\mathrm{Cl_2/Cl^-}$
variantes.contenu_markdown: An **inert platinum electrode** carries the electrons to and from the solution. Both ions are present in the solution at $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ (for example $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$), or the gas is bubbled at 1 atm over platinum in a solution of its ion. Cell diagram: $\mathrm{Pt\,|\,Fe^{2+}(aq),\,Fe^{3+}(aq)\;||\;Cu^{2+}(aq)\,|\,Cu(s)}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked whether a reaction with a positive $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}$ will actually happen, or what changes when concentrations change
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A positive $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}$ says only that the reaction is **feasible** under standard conditions. It says nothing about the **rate**: a reaction with a large positive value may still be extremely slow because its activation energy is high.

If conditions are not standard, the equilibrium $\mathrm{M^{n+} + ne^- \rightleftharpoons M}$ shifts (Le Chatelier). Lowering the concentration of $\mathrm{M^{n+}}$ moves the equilibrium to the left and makes the electrode potential more negative; raising it makes the potential more positive. A reaction with a small positive $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}$ can therefore be reversed by a change of concentration.

variantes.nom: Displacement of one metal by another
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked whether a metal displaces another metal ion from solution
variantes.contenu_markdown: A metal M displaces the ions of a metal N from solution if $E^{\ominus}(\mathrm{N^{n+}/N}) - E^{\ominus}(\mathrm{M^{m+}/M}) > 0$. For zinc and copper(II) ions: $+0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10\ \mathrm{V}$, so $\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \to Zn^{2+} + Cu}$ is feasible: zinc is the stronger reducing agent. The reverse reaction, copper in zinc ions, has $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = -1.10\ \mathrm{V}$ and does not happen.

sections.enonce_markdown: A cell is made from an aluminium electrode in $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ aluminium ions and a copper electrode in $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ copper(II) ions, joined by a salt bridge. Data: $\mathrm{Al^{3+}(aq) + 3e^- \rightleftharpoons Al(s)}$, $E^{\ominus} = -1.66\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons Cu(s)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.34\ \mathrm{V}$. (a) Identify the positive and negative electrodes and the direction of electron flow. (b) Write the half-equation at each electrode and the overall equation. (c) Calculate the standard emf of the cell.

etapes.justification: The more positive value is the positive electrode (reduction); the more negative value is the negative electrode (oxidation).
etapes.resultat_markdown: Copper ($+0.34\ \mathrm{V}$) is positive; aluminium ($-1.66\ \mathrm{V}$) is negative. Electrons flow in the wire from aluminium to copper.

etapes.action: Write the half-equation at each electrode.
etapes.justification: Oxidation takes place at the negative electrode, reduction at the positive one.

etapes.action: Balance the electrons and add the half-equations.
etapes.justification: The least common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6, so multiply the aluminium equation by 2 and the copper equation by 3.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $\mathrm{2Al(s) + 3Cu^{2+}(aq) \to 2Al^{3+}(aq) + 3Cu(s)}$ (6 electrons transferred; charge $+6$ on each side).

etapes.justification: Use $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\ominus}(\text{positive}) - E^{\ominus}(\text{negative})$ with the values as given in the table; the multiplication factors are not used.

etapes.action: Write the cell diagram and state feasibility.
etapes.justification: By convention the oxidation half-cell is written on the left and the salt bridge is shown by a double line.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Aluminium is the negative electrode, copper the positive electrode, the overall equation is $\mathrm{2Al + 3Cu^{2+} \to 2Al^{3+} + 3Cu}$ and the standard emf is **+2.00 V**.

items.erreur_markdown: "When the copper half-equation is multiplied by 3, its $E^{\ominus}$ becomes $3\times0.34 = 1.02\ \mathrm{V}$."
items.pourquoi_faux: Electrode potential is energy per unit charge, so it is an intensive quantity: it does not change when an equation is multiplied by a number.
items.correction_markdown: Always use the tabulated value: $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.34 - (-1.66) = +2.00\ \mathrm{V}$ for the aluminium-copper cell.

items.erreur_markdown: "The half-cell with the more negative $E^{\ominus}$ is the positive electrode, because it has a negative sign."
items.pourquoi_faux: Reduction occurs at the positive electrode, and it is the half-cell with the more positive $E^{\ominus}$ that is reduced. The negative electrode is where electrons are produced by oxidation.
items.correction_markdown: Positive electrode = more positive $E^{\ominus}$ (reduction). Negative electrode = more negative $E^{\ominus}$ (oxidation).

items.erreur_markdown: "The emf is positive, so the reaction will occur quickly."
items.pourquoi_faux: $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}$ predicts feasibility only under standard conditions. The rate depends on the activation energy, which the potential does not tell us.
items.correction_markdown: Say that the reaction is feasible (thermodynamically); whether it is fast needs kinetic information.

items.erreur_markdown: "The salt bridge lets electrons pass from one beaker to the other."
items.pourquoi_faux: Electrons travel only through the metal wire. The salt bridge contains mobile ions that balance the charges built up in the two beakers.
items.correction_markdown: Electrons flow through the external circuit; ions flow through the salt bridge, which completes the circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral.

items.erreur_markdown: "The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of 0.00 V because it was measured against zinc."
items.pourquoi_faux: The value 0.00 V is a definition, chosen as the zero of the scale. All other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.
items.correction_markdown: $E^{\ominus}(\mathrm{H^+/H_2}) = 0.00\ \mathrm{V}$ by definition, at 298 K, $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\mathrm{H^+}$ and 1 atm $\mathrm{H_2}$.

items.enonce_markdown: Data: $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons Ni(s)}$, $E^{\ominus} = -0.25\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons Cu(s)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.34\ \mathrm{V}$. A standard cell is built from these two half-cells. (a) State which electrode is positive. (b) Calculate the standard emf. (c) Write the overall cell reaction and the direction of electron flow in the external wire.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Copper has the more positive potential, so **copper is the positive electrode** and nickel the negative electrode.

(b) $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.34 - (-0.25) = $ **$+0.59\ \mathrm{V}$**.

(c) Oxidation at nickel: $\mathrm{Ni \to Ni^{2+} + 2e^-}$; reduction at copper: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \to Cu}$. Overall: **$\mathrm{Ni(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq) \to Ni^{2+}(aq) + Cu(s)}$**. Electrons flow in the wire **from nickel to copper**.

items.enonce_markdown: Data: $\mathrm{Br_2(aq) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2Br^-(aq)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +1.07\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq) + e^- \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}(aq)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.77\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{I_2(aq) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2I^-(aq)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.54\ \mathrm{V}$. Use these data to decide whether (i) bromine can oxidise iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions and (ii) iodine can oxidise iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions. Write the equation for any reaction that is feasible and state one reason why a feasible reaction might not be observed.
items.solution_markdown:
(i) For the cell with bromine as the oxidising agent: $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +1.07 - (+0.77) = $ **$+0.30\ \mathrm{V}$**. Positive, so the reaction is feasible: **$\mathrm{Br_2 + 2Fe^{2+} \to 2Br^- + 2Fe^{3+}}$** (2 electrons transferred, so the iron half-equation is doubled; the potentials are not).

(ii) With iodine: $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.54 - (+0.77) = $ **$-0.23\ \mathrm{V}$**. Negative, so iodine does **not** oxidise iron(II) ions under standard conditions. The reverse reaction, iron(III) oxidising iodide ions, is the feasible one.

A feasible reaction may not be observed if its rate is very slow (high activation energy), or if the conditions are not standard (for example much lower concentrations).

items.enonce_markdown: Data: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-(aq) + 8H^+(aq) + 5e^- \rightleftharpoons Mn^{2+}(aq) + 4H_2O(l)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +1.51\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{Cl_2(g) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2Cl^-(aq)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +1.36\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq) + e^- \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}(aq)}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.77\ \mathrm{V}$. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reaction between acidified manganate(VII) ions and chloride ions and calculate the standard emf. (b) Write the equation for the reaction between acidified manganate(VII) ions and iron(II) ions and calculate the standard emf. (c) In a titration, $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of an iron(II) solution needed $20.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.0200\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ potassium manganate(VII). Calculate the concentration of the iron(II) solution. (d) Suggest why hydrochloric acid is not used to acidify the titration mixture.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Manganate(VII) is reduced (5 electrons), chloride is oxidised (2 electrons); the lowest common multiple is 10 electrons: **$\mathrm{2MnO_4^- + 16H^+ + 10Cl^- \to 2Mn^{2+} + 8H_2O + 5Cl_2}$** (charge $+4$ on both sides). $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +1.51 - (+1.36) = $ **$+0.15\ \mathrm{V}$**: feasible, though only slightly.

(b) **$\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \to Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O}$** (charge $+17$ on both sides). $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +1.51 - (+0.77) = $ **$+0.74\ \mathrm{V}$**.

(c) $n(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}) = 0.0200\times0.0200 = 4.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}$. From the 1:5 ratio, $n(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}) = 5\times4.00\times10^{-4} = 2.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ in $0.0250\ \mathrm{dm^3}$, so $[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}] = 2.00\times10^{-3}/0.0250 = $ **$0.0800\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$**.

(d) The reaction in (a) has a positive emf, so manganate(VII) would also oxidise chloride ions from the hydrochloric acid and use up some of the titrant, making the volume too large and the result inaccurate. Dilute sulfuric acid is used instead.

items_markdown: E-standard is the emf of a half-cell against the standard hydrogen electrode (298 K, 1.00 mol per dm3, 1 atm); the SHE is defined as 0.00 V.
E-standard(cell) = E(positive electrode) minus E(negative electrode): the more positive half-cell is the positive electrode and is reduced.
Never multiply E-standard values when you multiply half-equations; electrons are balanced but potentials are not scaled.
A positive E-standard(cell) means the reaction is feasible under standard conditions, not that it is fast.
Electrons flow through the external wire from the negative to the positive electrode; ions move through the salt bridge.
Changing the concentration of an ion shifts the half-cell equilibrium: lower concentration of the oxidised form makes the potential more negative.
